appendices.title: Numbers and rules of thumb
appendices.intro: These are common guides, not laws. A value on the wrong side of a line is a prompt to look closer. The project workbook uses the same lines for its automatic review.
rows: Below 2.5 Å good; above 3.5 Å poor
Resolution describes the whole map; the pocket may be better or worse.
Shows the protocol can reproduce one known pose, not that it will rank new compounds correctly.
More negative is better; compare with the reference drug
The least reliable output. Large molecules score better by size alone, so also use ligand efficiency.
About 0.3 kcal/mol per heavy atom or more is considered efficient
A guide for comparing similar compounds.
MW ≤ 500, cLogP ≤ 5, HBD ≤ 5, HBA ≤ 10; two or more breaks is a concern
Many good drugs break it (for example natural products and drugs that use transporters).
0.5 is random; above 0.7 useful; above 0.9 very good
Depends strongly on the decoys chosen.
1 is random; above about 5 in the top 1% to 5% is good
The best possible value is limited by the share of actives in the library.
Above 40% usually good; 30 to 40% careful; below 30% twilight zone
Alignment quality matters as much as the number.
Copied angles look good even for a wrong template.
Above 90 very high; 70 to 90 confident; below 70 low
Check the binding-site residues, not the average.
0.1 or more counts as a real prediction; 0.000 is noise
Tools differ in scale; unusual compounds often score low.
Combines several kinds of evidence; high does not always mean direct contact.
Corrected p (FDR q) below 0.05, at least 2 genes
Depends on the background; state it.
1 to 2 fs; 2 fs only with constraints on bonds to hydrogen
Plateaus; about 1 to 3 Å for a folded protein
Depends on the protein and its flexible parts.
About 2 Å or less after fitting on the protein suggests a stable pose
At least 3 replicas; 100 ns is common for a first look
Slow events need much longer runs.
Use for ranking similar compounds, with an error

appendices.title: Formulae in plain words
appendices.intro: The calculations behind the modules, written so you can follow them without a maths text.
rows: RMSD = √( sum of (distance between matching atoms)² ÷ number of atoms )
The typical distance between two structures, in Å.
Docking score per atom, so that size does not flatter a compound.
Tc = shared features ÷ (features in A + features in B − shared features)
0 means nothing in common, 1 means identical fingerprints.
EF = (actives in top n ÷ n) ÷ (actives in library ÷ library size)
How much better than random the top of the list is.
Acid: neutral fraction = 1 ÷ (1 + 10^(pH − pKa)). Base: 1 ÷ (1 + 10^(pKa − pH))
Only the neutral form crosses membranes easily.
A quick estimate of aqueous solubility (Delaney 2004).
The elimination rate constant from the half-life.
Area under the concentration–time curve after a single dose.
Repeated doses build up to a steady state; dosing every half-life doubles the level
expected RMSD ≈ 0.40 × exp(1.87 × fraction of different residues)
Expected error of the core of a homology model from sequence identity.
Share of all shortest paths between pairs of nodes that pass through a node
P(X ≥ k) = Σ C(K,i)·C(N−K,n−i) ÷ C(N,n), for i from k to n
Chance of at least k pathway genes in a list of n by luck.
q(i) = p(i) × m ÷ i for the i-th smallest of m p-values, made non-decreasing from the top
v(t+½dt) = v(t) + ½·a(t)·dt; x(t+dt) = x(t) + v(t+½dt)·dt; recompute a; v(t+dt) = v(t+½dt) + ½·a(t+dt)·dt
Moves atoms one time step from their forces.
Attraction at a distance, strong repulsion up close.
T = 2 × kinetic energy ÷ (3 × number of particles × k_B)
Split the run into blocks, take the mean of each, use the spread of block means as the error
Gives an honest error for correlated frames.

appendices.title: Ten questions to ask of any CADD result
appendices.intro: A habit that works for every module and every software.
items: What exactly was the question, and does this result answer it?
Which structure, compounds and settings were used? Can someone repeat it?
Was there a control (a known drug or known active)? How did it behave?
Was the method tested before use (redocking, known actives against decoys, validation of the model)?
Is this a number or a picture? Have I looked at the picture?
Are the units and the direction clear (is more negative better)?
How big is the uncertainty? Is there an error, a repeat, a second method?
What would I expect if the result were wrong? Does this look like that?
What does this result not show?
What is the cheapest experiment that could prove it wrong?
